title: Lazy Propagation
tagline: Range updates in O(log n) by deferring work until a node is actually visited.

intuition.analogy: A manager told 'give everyone on your team a raise' doesn't immediately walk to each desk. They note 'pending: +10% for my team' and only push it down when someone actually asks about a specific sub-team.
paragraphs: A plain segment tree updates one element at a time. To add a value to a whole RANGE without touching every leaf, lazy propagation stores a pending update at each node and applies it only when necessary.

When a range update fully covers a node, you update that node's aggregate and stash the pending delta in its 'lazy' tag instead of descending. Later, when a query or update needs the node's children, you 'push down' the stored delta first.
This keeps both range updates and range queries at O(log n). The bookkeeping — applying a tag to a node's value and propagating it to children correctly — is the part to internalise.
intuition.keyIdea: Store a pending update on fully-covered nodes; push it to children only when you must descend.

steps.title: Add a lazy tag
steps.detail: Each node has a pending value (e.g. 'add x to this whole range') not yet pushed to children.

steps.title: Apply on full cover
steps.detail: When a range update fully covers a node, adjust its aggregate (e.g. sum += x · rangeLen) and add x to its lazy tag; do not recurse.

steps.title: Push down before descending
steps.detail: Before recursing into children (for a partial update or query), apply the node's lazy tag to both children and clear it.

complexity.timeReason: Full-cover nodes stop recursion; only O(log n) boundary nodes are split.
complexity.spaceReason: An extra lazy array parallel to the tree.

pitfalls: Always push down before recursing into children, or stale values leak.
The tag must combine correctly (adds accumulate; assignments overwrite).
Scale aggregates by the segment length when the update is additive.

dryRun.clickMoment: The range update never touched the individual leaves — it parked '+5' on node [0,3]. Only the later query forced that +5 to trickle down exactly where it was needed.

problems.title: Range Update Range Sum
problems.statement: Add to a range; query range sums.
problems.hint: Lazy segment tree with additive tags.

approach: Range add + range sum needs lazy propagation: each node stores its subtree sum and a pending 'add' to push down on demand.
On a range update, mark fully-covered nodes lazily (sum += add·len) instead of touching every leaf; push the lazy tag to children only when you must recurse deeper.

problems.title: Range Assignment + Sum
problems.statement: Assign a value to a range; query sums.
problems.hint: Lazy tag that overwrites rather than adds.

approach: Range assignment (set every element in [l,r] to v) plus range sum. The lazy tag is now an assignment, not an increment.
A covered node's sum becomes v·len and its lazy is set to v. push() copies the assignment to children and clears it. Use a sentinel to distinguish 'no pending assignment'.

problems.title: My Calendar III
problems.hint: Range +1 with lazy propagation (or a difference array).

approach: We need the maximum number of simultaneously overlapping bookings (a k-booking). A difference-array over event points captures overlaps.

Increment a counter at each start and decrement at each end in an ordered map; sweep keeping a running sum and track its maximum. (A lazy segment tree over compressed coordinates achieves the same in O(log n) per booking.)

complexity.time: O(n^2) sweep / O(n log n) ordered map

problems.title: Range Module
problems.hint: Segment tree with range assign + lazy, or interval set.

approach: Maintain a set of disjoint covered intervals in an ordered map keyed by start. addRange merges overlaps, removeRange splits them, queryRange checks containment.
This range-tracking is the same problem lazy segment trees solve; an ordered map is the clean balanced-tree implementation.

problems.title: Number of Flowers in Full Bloom
problems.statement: Count active intervals at query times.

approach: For each person at time t, the number of flowers in bloom is (flowers that started by t) - (flowers that ended before t).
Sort start times and end times separately. Each query is two binary searches: bisect_right(starts, t) - bisect_left(ends, t).

codes.title: solution.cpp
solution.py
codes.source:
import bisect
class Solution:
    def fullBloomFlowers(self, flowers: list[list[int]], people: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        starts = sorted(f[0] for f in flowers)
        ends = sorted(f[1] for f in flowers)
        res = []
        for t in people:
            opened = bisect.bisect_right(starts, t)
            closed = bisect.bisect_left(ends, t)
            res.append(opened - closed)
        return res
